before.content_html:
The Victorian Obsession with Respectability

Robert Louis Stevenson published The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, at the height of the Victorian era. Victorian society was obsessed with respectability: gentlemen were expected to be rational, self-controlled, and morally upright in public. But beneath this polished surface, Victorian London harboured a hidden world of vice — prostitution, opium dens, gambling, and poverty. Stevenson’s novella explores this gap between public respectability and private desire.

The concept of duality was central to Victorian thought. Scientists, philosophers, and theologians all debated whether human nature was fundamentally good or evil. Stevenson dramatises this debate through Jekyll’s experiment: what if you could physically separate the two sides of your nature? The answer, the novella argues, is catastrophe — because good and evil are not separate entities but inseparable parts of the same person.

Key Fact

Victorian gentlemen maintained strict public respectability while often indulging private vices. Stevenson uses Jekyll’s experiment to expose this hypocrisy: Jekyll does not create evil — he releases the evil that was already inside him. Hyde is not a separate person but the part of Jekyll that society forced him to suppress. The novella argues that repression, not human nature, is the true danger.

Science and Religion

The 1880s were a period of intense conflict between science and religion. Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) had challenged the biblical creation story and suggested that humans were descended from apes — an idea that horrified many Victorians. Hyde’s frequent description in animalistic terms (“like a monkey,” “snarled,” “ape-like fury”) connects him to Darwin’s theory: Hyde represents the primitive, animal nature that evolution revealed beneath the civilised surface.

Victorian readers feared degeneration — the idea that civilisation could go backwards, with humans reverting to a primitive state. Hyde embodies this fear: he is smaller than Jekyll (suggesting a less evolved form), described as “troglodytic” (cave-dweller), and provokes an instinctive revulsion in everyone who sees him. Characters struggle to describe what is wrong with Hyde: Enfield says he gave “a strong feeling of deformity,” though he cannot identify any specific feature. This indefinable wrongness suggests Hyde represents something beyond physical appearance — he is the degenerate self that Victorian society desperately wanted to deny.

Jekyll’s experiment can be read as a metaphor for the danger of scientific progress without moral restraint. He uses chemistry to achieve what nature would not allow: the separation of good and evil. But the experiment goes wrong because the separation is unnatural. Stevenson warns that science, like any form of power, requires ethical boundaries.

London as a Dual City

Stevenson sets the novella in London, a city that perfectly embodies Victorian duality. The respectable streets of the West End existed alongside the poverty and crime of the East End. Jekyll’s house has two faces: a handsome front door on a respectable street and a sinister back entrance (the “door” of Chapter 1) on a rundown lane. This architectural duality mirrors Jekyll’s psychological duality — the public face and the private shame are literally two sides of the same building.

Stevenson grew up in Edinburgh, a city with a literal split personality: the respectable New Town above and the cramped, vice-ridden Old Town below. He also knew about the real-life case of Deacon Brodie, an 18th-century Edinburgh cabinetmaker who was a respectable citizen by day and a burglar by night. These biographical connections help explain why duality fascinated Stevenson: he lived in a world where the gap between public and private selves was not just a literary idea but a daily reality.

Stevenson reportedly dreamed the central scene of the novella (the transformation) and wrote the first draft in three days. His wife Fanny criticised it for being too much of an adventure story, so he burned the manuscript and rewrote it as the psychological allegory we know today.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s house has a respectable front entrance and a sinister back door — two faces of the same building, just as Jekyll and Hyde are two faces of the same person. This architectural symbolism runs throughout the novella: Victorian London itself has a public face of respectability and a hidden world of vice.

before.content_html:
Chapter 1: The Door and Enfield’s Story

The novella opens with two respectable gentlemen, Mr Utterson (a lawyer) and his kinsman Mr Enfield, walking through London. They pass a sinister door on a rundown street, and Enfield tells a strange story: he once witnessed a man “calmly trampl[e] over a child’s body” at a street corner. The man was Hyde. The crowd surrounded him, and Hyde paid compensation through a cheque signed by the respectable Dr Jekyll. Enfield’s reaction to Hyde is visceral: “I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight.”

Stevenson uses mystery as his primary structural device. The reader, like Utterson, is given pieces of a puzzle without the full picture. We know Hyde is connected to Jekyll but not how. We know the door leads to Jekyll’s laboratory but not why Hyde uses it. The first four chapters build a web of second-hand narration: Enfield tells Utterson, Utterson investigates, but nobody speaks to Jekyll directly. This narrative structure mirrors the Victorian culture of secrecy — gentlemen do not ask uncomfortable questions.

Key Fact

Hyde tramples a young girl “calmly” — without remorse or hesitation. The word “calmly” is crucial: it shows that Hyde’s violence is not passionate rage but cold indifference to human suffering. He treats the child as though she does not exist. This establishes Hyde as a figure without empathy or conscience — the purely selfish part of human nature unleashed.

Chapter 2: Utterson’s Investigation

Utterson reads Jekyll’s will and discovers that everything is left to Hyde — including the provision that if Jekyll “disappears for any period exceeding three calendar months,” Hyde inherits. This alarming clause suggests either blackmail or something worse. Utterson visits Dr Lanyon, Jekyll’s old friend, who dismisses Jekyll’s recent scientific work as “unscientific balderdash.” The disagreement between the two doctors hints that Jekyll has crossed a moral boundary that Lanyon refuses to follow.

Utterson stakes out the sinister door and finally meets Hyde. His reaction is the same indefinable revulsion that every character experiences: “Mr Hyde was pale and dwarfish, he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” Hyde produces a “disgusting” impression that Utterson cannot explain: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic.” The word troglodytic links Hyde to prehistoric humanity, reinforcing the degeneration theme.

Notice that characters consistently cannot describe what is wrong with Hyde. This is Stevenson’s deliberate technique: by making Hyde’s evil indefinable, he makes it universal. Hyde does not look like a specific type of villain — he embodies a feeling of wrongness that everyone recognises but nobody can articulate. In the exam, this is a powerful AO2 point about Stevenson’s language choices.

Chapter 3: Jekyll’s Reassurance

Utterson confronts Jekyll, who dismisses his concerns: “I can be rid of Mr Hyde… whenever I choose.” This is deeply ironic because the reader later learns that Jekyll is already losing control. Jekyll’s confidence is the confidence of an addict who believes he can stop at any time. Stevenson uses proleptic irony throughout: statements that seem reassuring on first reading become ominous once the truth is revealed.

Chapter 4: The Carew Murder

Hyde’s violence escalates dramatically. He murders Sir Danvers Carew, a respected MP, in a frenzied attack witnessed by a maidservant: “Mr Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth. And next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattered.” The language is extraordinarily violent: “ape-like fury,” “trampling,” “bones audibly shattering.” Stevenson moves from the cold trampling of a child to a savage murder, showing Hyde’s escalating loss of control.

Carew is described as “an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair” who approaches Hyde “with a very pretty manner of politeness.” The contrast between Carew’s gentleness and Hyde’s savagery is absolute. Carew represents everything that Victorian respectability values: age, beauty, courtesy, and public service. Hyde’s destruction of him symbolises the assault of the primitive, selfish self on civilised values.

The maidservant who witnesses the murder does so by moonlight — she is at an upstairs window, looking down. This vertical perspective (observer above, crime below) mirrors the structure of Jekyll’s house and Victorian society itself: respectability lives upstairs, while violence happens in the streets below.

Key Fact

The Carew murder is described with escalating violence: “with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattered.” “Ape-like” links to degeneration, “trampling” echoes the child incident (showing escalation), and “bones audibly shattering” uses sound imagery to make the violence disturbingly real.

before.content_html:
Chapter 5: After the Murder

After the Carew murder, Jekyll appears to reform. He resumes his charitable work, becomes sociable, and seems healthier. For two months, he avoids the potion and Hyde disappears. But Stevenson shows this apparent recovery is fragile. Jekyll has not conquered Hyde — he has simply stopped taking the drug. The desire remains. Jekyll describes the temptation as “the animal within me licking the chops of memory.” This metaphor is central: Hyde is not a separate creature but an appetite — a hunger that grows stronger the longer it is denied.

Then, sitting on a park bench in January, Jekyll transforms into Hyde without the potion. This is the novella’s most terrifying turning point. The transformation has become involuntary. Jekyll can no longer choose when to be Hyde — Hyde is asserting independence, growing stronger each time he is released. The power balance has shifted: “Hyde’s powers had grown with the sickliness of Jekyll.”

Key Fact

The involuntary transformation marks the point of no return. Jekyll can no longer control when Hyde appears. Stevenson uses this to argue that evil, once indulged, grows stronger: “Hyde’s powers had grown with the sickliness of Jekyll.” The relationship between Jekyll and Hyde has reversed — Hyde is now the dominant personality, and Jekyll is the one fighting for survival.

Chapter 6: Lanyon’s Decline

Dr Lanyon, once a healthy and jovial man, suddenly falls ill and dies within weeks. His decline is caused by something he has witnessed but refuses to discuss: “I have had a shock… and I shall never recover.” Stevenson withholds the details until Lanyon’s letter in Chapter 9, building suspense through gaps in information. Lanyon represents the rational, conventional Victorian mind: he cannot process what he has seen because it violates everything he believes about science and human nature.

Utterson and Enfield see Jekyll at an upstairs window. He begins to talk to them, then a look of “abject terror and despair” crosses his face and he slams the window shut. The two men walk away in horrified silence: “They were both pale; and there was an answering horror in their eyes.” Stevenson does not explain what happened — was Jekyll transforming? The reader is left to imagine, which is more disturbing than any explicit description.

The window scene is significant because it is the only time other characters witness Jekyll’s transformation (or near-transformation) in real time. The “answering horror” in Utterson and Enfield’s eyes suggests they have glimpsed something they cannot consciously acknowledge. Stevenson uses their silence as a metaphor for Victorian society’s refusal to confront the truths it already half-knows.

Chapter 8: The Last Night

Jekyll’s servant Poole arrives at Utterson’s door in a state of terror. He believes his master has been murdered because the voice coming from the locked laboratory sounds different: “That’s not Jekyll’s voice — it’s Hyde’s!” Utterson and Poole break down the door and find Hyde’s body, dead by suicide, still twitching, with a phial of poison in his hand. Jekyll is nowhere to be found. The suspense reaches its peak: where is Jekyll? The answer comes only in the final two chapters, through Lanyon’s narrative and Jekyll’s full statement.

The locked door of the laboratory is the novella’s most important symbol. It separates the known from the unknown, the public from the private, the respectable from the terrible. Throughout the story, characters approach this door but stop short of breaking it open — just as Victorian society approached uncomfortable truths but refused to confront them. When Utterson finally breaks it down, the mystery is resolved, but the cost is total: Jekyll is gone, Lanyon is dead, and the truth destroys the illusion of respectable normality.

The scene also uses Gothic tension: the servants huddled in the hallway, the strange voice behind the door, Poole’s whispered fear. Stevenson combines detective fiction with Gothic horror, making the reader both investigator and terrified witness.

Key Fact

The locked laboratory door symbolises Victorian secrecy — the refusal to confront uncomfortable truths. Characters approach but do not open it. When Utterson finally breaks it down, he discovers that Jekyll and Hyde are one person — that the respectable doctor and the savage murderer cannot be separated. The truth, once exposed, destroys everything.

before.content_html:
Dr Henry Jekyll

Jekyll is a wealthy, respected doctor who appears to be a model Victorian gentleman. He is “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something of a slyish cast perhaps, but every mark of capacity and kindness.” The word “slyish” is crucial — even in this positive description, Stevenson hints at something hidden. Jekyll’s tragedy is not that he is evil but that he is human: he contains both good and evil and cannot accept this duality. His experiment is an attempt to be respectable and indulge his desires — to have it both ways without moral consequences.

Jekyll is ultimately a tragic figure. His flaw is not vice but the desire to escape moral accountability. He wants to sin without guilt, to be Hyde without being Hyde’s consequences. His confession reveals genuine self-knowledge (“I was in no sense a hypocrite”) but also self-deception (“I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose”). The gap between his self-knowledge and his self-deception is what destroys him.

Key Fact

Jekyll has genuine self-knowledge (“both sides of me were in dead earnest”) but also dangerous self-deception (“I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose”). He understands his duality intellectually but cannot control it practically. This makes him a tragic figure: he sees the truth but cannot act on it. His experiment is an attempt to cheat morality, and it destroys him.

Mr Edward Hyde

Hyde is described through other characters’ reactions because Stevenson never gives a detailed physical description. He is “pale and dwarfish,” gives an “impression of deformity without any nameable malformation,” and provokes instant revulsion. His violence escalates from cold indifference (trampling the child) to savage fury (the Carew murder). Hyde represents the id — the selfish, instinctive part of human nature freed from conscience.

Utterson is described as “austere with himself” — he suppresses his own pleasures (he drinks gin to mortify his taste for wine, and has not visited a theatre for twenty years). He represents the ideal Victorian gentleman: loyal, discreet, and restrained. But his very discretion is part of the problem. He suspects something is wrong with Jekyll for months but does not ask the right questions because Victorian propriety forbids intrusion into another gentleman’s private affairs.

Utterson also functions as the reader’s proxy: we discover information as he does. His rational, legal mind makes him a reliable narrator, but his Victorian restraint means he cannot see what is right in front of him. Stevenson uses Utterson to show how respectability itself becomes an obstacle to truth.

Lanyon dismissed Jekyll’s work as “unscientific balderdash” before the events of the novella. He represents conventional Victorian science — empirical, cautious, and unwilling to explore dangerous territory. When he witnesses the transformation, the shock kills him. Lanyon is Stevenson’s comment on the limits of the conventional Victorian worldview: it can function only as long as certain truths remain hidden. Once exposed, it shatters.

Lanyon and Jekyll are foils: Jekyll pushes beyond accepted boundaries while Lanyon stays safely within them. Both are destroyed — Jekyll by his recklessness and Lanyon by the truth he refused to consider. Stevenson suggests there is no safe position: ignoring human duality is as dangerous as confronting it.

Key Fact

Each character represents a different response to duality: Jekyll (attempts to separate good and evil), Hyde (evil without conscience), Utterson (refuses to look too closely), Lanyon (destroyed by the truth he cannot accept). Together, they explore the Victorian dilemma: how do you live with the knowledge that civilised people contain primitive impulses?

before.content_html:
London as a Character

Stevenson’s London is a city of contrasts. Respectable streets give way to “dingy” lanes without warning. Fog descends and lifts unpredictably, concealing and revealing. The fog is not just weather — it is a metaphor for the obscured truth that pervades the novella. When Utterson investigates, he moves through “a great chocolate-coloured pall lowered over heaven… the fog still slept on the wing of the morning.” The language of sleep and darkness suggests a city that does not want to see clearly.

Settings in the novella consistently reflect the theme of duality. Scenes of respectability are disrupted by violence: the Carew murder happens on a moonlit street, the trampling occurs at a busy corner. Stevenson shows that evil does not confine itself to dark alleys — it erupts in public spaces, breaking through the surface of civilised life.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s house is the novella’s most important setting. The handsome front door opens onto a respectable street; the sinister back door (where Hyde enters) opens onto a rundown lane. The two entrances represent Jekyll’s dual nature — the public face of respectability and the private entrance for vice. The laboratory connecting them is where the transformation occurs: the space where public and private selves meet.

Narrative Structure: Multiple Perspectives

Stevenson uses an unusual narrative structure. The first eight chapters are third-person narration focused through Utterson. Chapters 9 and 10 switch to first-person accounts from Lanyon and Jekyll respectively. This structure creates a layered revelation: the reader gets the “outside view” first (what people see) and the “inside view” last (what Jekyll feels). The truth is discovered in reverse — the explanation comes after the events, forcing the reader to re-evaluate everything they thought they knew.

The novella’s characters are almost entirely male. There are no significant female characters: the maidservant witnesses the Carew murder, and the child and the old woman are brief presences. This homosocial world reflects Victorian gentlemen’s culture of clubs, professional partnerships, and male friendships. It also intensifies the theme of secrecy: these men are bound by codes of discretion that prevent them from asking each other uncomfortable questions.

Some critics read the absence of women as significant for what it conceals. Jekyll’s “undignified pleasures” are never specified, and Victorian readers would have understood the implication: the vices of gentlemen were sexual, financial, or narcotic — but always hidden. Stevenson’s vagueness is deliberate: by not naming Jekyll’s sins, he makes them universal.

Gothic Techniques

Stevenson employs classic Gothic techniques: dark settings, locked doors, mysterious sounds, and a sense of building dread. But he adapts the Gothic for a modern urban setting. The terror of Jekyll and Hyde is not supernatural — it is psychological and scientific. The most frightening element is not a ghost or a monster but the discovery that the monster lives inside the respectable doctor next door.

Throughout the novella, characters use the language of concealment. Enfield tells Utterson: “I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.” Utterson reflects: “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek.” Even when characters resolve to investigate, they wrap their intentions in wordplay and deflection. Stevenson shows that Victorian language itself is a form of concealment — a way of talking about things without naming them.

This linguistic concealment mirrors the novella’s larger argument: Victorian society has developed sophisticated ways of hiding its dual nature. The polished language, the codes of propriety, the refusal to ask uncomfortable questions — these are not just social habits but defence mechanisms against the terrifying truth that civilised people contain savage impulses.

Key Fact

Stevenson’s narrative structure (outside view first, inside view last) forces the reader to discover the truth in reverse. His language of concealment (characters refusing to name what they see) mirrors Victorian society’s defence against uncomfortable truths. Both techniques make the reader experience the same discomfort as the characters: we know something is wrong but cannot quite name it.

before.description: Key themes of Jekyll and Hyde with exam strategy for Eduqas Component 2 Section B.
before.content_html:
Theme: Duality of Human Nature

The novella’s central argument is that every person contains both good and evil. Jekyll states: “man is not truly one, but truly two.” He attempts to separate these natures through science, but the experiment proves that they are inseparable. Hyde is not a foreign intruder but the part of Jekyll that society forced him to suppress. The novella argues that repression is more dangerous than acknowledgement: pretending evil does not exist makes it stronger, while recognising it honestly might allow it to be managed.

This theme connects to Victorian rationalism: the idea that civilised behaviour is a permanent achievement rather than a constant effort. Stevenson challenges this: civilisation is a thin veneer, and beneath it lies the same primitive nature that Darwin’s theory revealed. Hyde’s animalistic descriptions (“ape-like fury,” “troglodytic”) remind Victorian readers that evolution did not eliminate the animal — it only covered it with a suit and top hat.

Key Fact

Jekyll believes “man is not truly one, but truly two” and attempts to separate the two. But Stevenson’s novella shows this is impossible: good and evil are inseparable parts of the same person. Hyde cannot be permanently controlled or eliminated because he is Jekyll. The novella argues that managing duality requires honest self-knowledge, not scientific shortcuts.

Theme: Reputation and Secrecy

Every character in the novella guards his reputation obsessively. Jekyll hides Hyde behind a separate identity. Utterson refuses to gossip. Enfield’s rule is “the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.” This culture of secrecy is presented as both symptom and cause of the problem: Victorian gentlemen cannot acknowledge their darker impulses because doing so would destroy their social standing. The result is that secrets fester, hidden selves grow stronger, and the eventual exposure is catastrophic.

Jekyll’s experiment represents science without ethical boundaries. He uses chemistry to achieve what nature forbids: the separation of good and evil. But the experiment is driven by selfish motives (freedom from moral accountability), and its consequences are disastrous. Stevenson was writing during a period of rapid scientific advance, and the novella warns that progress without morality leads to destruction.

Lanyon and Jekyll represent two attitudes to science: Lanyon is cautious and conventional, Jekyll is reckless and innovative. Both are inadequate. Stevenson suggests that science needs both ambition and restraint — a lesson that resonates far beyond the Victorian period.

Most 19th-century prose questions give you a printed extract and ask you to write about the extract and the novella as a whole. You will be assessed against the standard GCSE English Literature assessment objectives — AO1 (response with quotations), AO2 (language, form, structure), AO3 (context), and AO4 (written accuracy). Spend a few minutes annotating the extract before writing 4–5 developed paragraphs. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact mark weightings and timings.

Quotation bank: “Man is not truly one, but truly two” (duality). “The animal within me licking the chops of memory” (temptation). “With ape-like fury” (degeneration). “Deformity without nameable malformation” (indefinable evil). “Both sides were in dead earnest” (genuine duality). “I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose” (self-deception). Learn all six and practise linking each to multiple themes.

Connecting Themes

The genius of Jekyll and Hyde is that all themes connect. Duality drives the experiment, which raises questions about science and morality. The experiment must be kept secret because Victorian respectability cannot tolerate the truth about human nature. The secrecy enables Hyde’s crimes, which escalate because evil grows when indulged. The delayed revelation mirrors Victorian society’s refusal to confront what it already knows. In the exam, showing how themes interconnect demonstrates the sophisticated understanding that earns the highest marks.

Key Fact

The four main themes (duality, secrecy/reputation, science/morality, and the nature of evil) are interconnected: duality creates the desire for separation, the experiment requires secrecy, secrecy enables escalation, and escalation proves that evil cannot be controlled. Showing these connections in the exam demonstrates whole-text understanding.
